title: An Ancient Nuclear War?
yt_title: Was There an Ancient Nuclear War? Five Clues, Weighed
verdict_scope: An ancient nuclear war, as read from these five physical clues: Ruled out (each clue has an observed natural or human cause, and the fingerprint a war would leave, plutonium and fission products in dated layers, has never been reported). Graded separately in the weighing: the yellow glass as melted by a cosmic impact or airburst about 29 million years ago: Strong evidence (shock minerals, melt temperatures, shocked bedrock; no source crater confirmed); the Wabar craters as an iron meteorite impact a few centuries ago: Established; the Mohenjo-daro skeletons as victims of one sudden blast: Ruled out (found at different levels, the excavators' own records); radioactive bones: Awaiting evidence (no measurement ever published); vitrified walls as burnt timber-laced ramparts: Established (reproduced experimentally), why they burned: Open question; Oklo as a natural reactor: Established. The epics some writers read as weapons are not graded.
hook: Was there a nuclear war before history?
end_line: A splash of cosmic fire, older than any war.

description:
A beetle of yellow-green glass glows on a jewel made for Tutankhamun. The same glass lies in the Sahara, melted about 29 million years ago. Some modern writers read it, with the black glass of Arabia, the skeletons of Mohenjo-daro, Scotland's melted forts and the natural reactors of Oklo, as traces of a nuclear war before history.

We weigh each clue with the claim at its strongest: what melted the desert, what the Wabar craters hold and how old they are, what Mohenjo-daro's excavators actually recorded (and the radiation measurement nobody has published), how a wood fire melts a wall, and how a reactor ran by itself two billion years ago. The yellow glass as a cosmic impact: Strong evidence. Wabar's meteorite, the burnt timber-laced walls and Oklo's natural reactor: Established. One blast at Mohenjo-daro: Ruled out; radioactive bones: Awaiting evidence. An ancient nuclear war: Ruled out. The epics some writers read as weapons are sacred to many, and are not graded here.

facts_added.fact: Patrick A. Clayton of the Desert Survey of Egypt found the glass on 29 December 1932, lying on Nubian sandstone in the sand-free corridors between the north-south dune ranges of the south-western Great Sand Sea; it was scattered over an area at least 80 by 25 km; lumps reached up to 10 lb (about 4.5 kg); analysis gave 97.58% silica; at least 10% of small pieces showed old fractures that may be human working.
facts_added.source: Clayton & Spencer 1934, Mineralogical Magazine 23: 501-508, doi:10.1180/minmag.1934.023.145.01

facts_added.fact: The dunes of the area are linear, trending almost exactly north-south, up to 100 m high and tens of km long, separated by corridors 2 to 5 km wide; a handaxe made of the glass was found there on 23 June 1979.
The glass is about 29 million years old (fission-track and argon dating); fission tracks are the damage trails left by the spontaneous fission of uranium atoms in the glass, counted to give its age.
facts_added.source: Cavosie & Koeberl 2019 (about 29 Ma), doi:10.1130/G45974.1; Bigazzi & de Michele and Horn et al. in Silica '96 (de Michele ed. 1997, Pyramids, Segrate)

facts_added.fact: Zircon grains in the glass preserve evidence of former reidite, a high-pressure form of zircon that needs shock pressures above 30 GPa; the authors conclude the glass formed in a crater-forming impact rather than an airburst.
facts_added.source: Cavosie & Koeberl 2019, Geology 47: 609-612, doi:10.1130/G45974.1

facts_added.fact: The melts that made the glass were above 2,750 degrees C, approaching the boiling point of silica, and orthorhombic zirconia records pressures above 13.5 GPa.
facts_added.source: Kovaleva et al. 2023, American Mineralogist 108: 1906-1923, doi:10.2138/am-2022-8759

facts_added.fact: Quartz in bedrock in the glass area carries shock features (planar fractures and planar deformation features) formed at at least 16 GPa; the authors infer a physical impact, not just an airburst, and a crater almost completely eroded since.
facts_added.source: Koeberl & Ferriere 2019, Meteoritics & Planetary Science 54: 2398-2408, doi:10.1111/maps.13250

facts_added.fact: The 31 km Kebira structure, proposed in 2007 as the glass's source crater, failed field and isotope tests: Orti et al. (2008) found no clear evidence of impact, and the oxygen isotopes of its sandstones do not match the glass.
facts_added.source: Longinelli et al. 2011, Meteoritics & Planetary Science 46: 218-227, doi:10.1111/j.1945-5100.2010.01147.x; Orti et al. 2008, Meteoritics & Planetary Science

facts_added.fact: Airburst models show that a large low-altitude airburst could melt desert sand without leaving a crater; the Libyan Desert Glass was one of the cases discussed.
facts_added.source: Boslough & Crawford 2008, International Journal of Impact Engineering 35: 1441-1448, doi:10.1016/j.ijimpeng.2008.07.053

facts_added.fact: The pectoral with the scarab (Carter object 267d, Cairo JE 61884) came from casket 267 in the Treasury, cleared in the 1926-27 season (the casket was moved to the laboratory on 29-30 October 1926); Carter published it in 1933; the scarab, earlier described as chalcedony, was identified as Libyan Desert Glass by the mineralogist Vincenzo de Michele (noticed in 1996, published in 1998).
facts_added.source: Griffith Institute, object record 267d and Carter's journal of the 5th season; Carter 1933, The Tomb of Tut.ankh.Amen vol. III (Cassell); de Michele 1998, Sahara 10: 107-109

facts_added.fact: Trinitite, the glass of the Trinity test of 16 July 1945, contains melted bits of the bomb and its tower and radionuclides formed in the detonation (still measurable decades later: americium-241, caesium-137, europium-152 and plutonium).
facts_added.source: Eby et al. 2010, Geology Today 26: 180-185, doi:10.1111/j.1365-2451.2010.00767.x; Parekh et al. 2006, Journal of Environmental Radioactivity 85: 103-120, doi:10.1016/j.jenvrad.2005.01.017

facts_added.fact: Philby reached the Wabar site in 1932 while crossing the Rub' al Khali in search of the legendary city and first took the site for volcanic; the craters are 116 m and 64 m across (plus an 11 m crater); the impactor was an iron meteorite of at least 3,500 tonnes, and the explosion released about as much energy as the Hiroshima bomb.
facts_added.source: Wynn & Shoemaker 1998, Scientific American 279(5): 64-71, doi:10.1038/scientificamerican1198-64; Philby 1933, The Empty Quarter (Constable)

facts_added.fact: The largest iron mass, the Camel's Hump, weighs about 2 tonnes (about 2,040 kg in meteorite catalogues) and was recovered in the 1960s.
facts_added.source: Gnos et al. 2013, doi:10.1111/maps.12218; meteorite catalogue entries for Wabar

facts_added.fact: Luminescence dating of the impactite and the sand under it gives an age of 290 plus or minus 38 years for the Wabar craters.
facts_added.source: Prescott et al. 2004, Journal of Geophysical Research 109: E01008, doi:10.1029/2003JE002136

facts_added.fact: In March 2008 only two Wabar craters were visible; Philby-A was completely covered by sand; the seif dunes migrate about 1 to 2 m a year; the black impact glass is a mixture of dune sand and iron meteorite, with nickel in unoxidized metal droplets; coesite and stishovite and shocked quartz occur in shock-lithified sand.
facts_added.source: Gnos et al. 2013, Meteoritics & Planetary Science 48: 2000-2014, doi:10.1111/maps.12218

facts_added.fact: Nine years of excavation at Mohenjo-daro (1922-31) yielded some 37 skeletons in non-burial contexts, in a few groups: 14 in Room 74 of House V (HR area), 9 in Block 10A of the DK area (at least five of them children), 6 in a lane of the VS area, 3 in a courtyard and 1 in 'Deadman Lane'; the excavators disagreed (Hargreaves saw a tragedy, Marshall thought the 14 had been intentionally interred within a few hours of death); Dales found the remains not demonstrably contemporary: four of the fourteen lay above the ruins of the room's southern wall, and the courtyard group and the Deadman Lane skeleton lay in debris laid down after those places fell into disuse; a couple seemed to have been killed where they lay, but most were careless burials, with no destruction level over the latest city and no sign of extensive burning.
facts_added.source: Dales 1964, Expedition 6(3): 36-43; Marshall 1931 (Probsthain); Mackay 1938 (Government of India)

facts_added.fact: Wheeler read the Mohenjo-daro skeletons as victims of a massacre by invaders ('Indra stands accused').
facts_added.source: Wheeler 1947, Ancient India 3: 58-130; discussed in Dales 1964

facts_added.fact: No measurement of radioactivity in the Mohenjo-daro skeletons has been reported in any excavation report or scientific paper; the claim appears in popular books from the 1960s and 1970s without a laboratory, a sample or a figure.
facts_added.source: Absence in Marshall 1931, Mackay 1938 and Dales 1964; the claim's history traced by J. Colavito (blog post, 16 May 2018) from Soviet popular literature of the 1960s (Gorbovsky) to C. Berlitz (1972)

facts_added.fact: Harappan cities deurbanised after about 3,900 years ago as monsoon rains declined; the process was gradual and regionally varied, with settlement shifting east, not a sudden collapse.

About 200 vitrified hillforts are known in Europe (about 3% of Scotland's hillforts); vitrification needs about 1,000 to 1,250 degrees C (as low as 850 to 900 with long heating); explanations include destruction by enemies, ritual decommissioning and deliberate firing to strengthen walls.
facts_added.source: McCloy et al. 2021, Scientific Reports 11: 1272, doi:10.1038/s41598-020-80485-w

facts_added.fact: On 11 March 1937 at Plean Colliery, Stirlingshire, Childe and the mining engineer Wallace Thorneycroft built a timber-laced wall 12 ft long, 6 ft wide and 6 ft high (basalt rubble core, fireclay brick faces, about a ton of pit-props) and set it alight at 11 a.m.; it was hottest five hours later and still smouldering the next morning, 20 hours after it was lit; the rubble core vitrified, with casts of timber and inclusions of charcoal.
facts_added.source: Childe & Thorneycroft 1938, Proceedings of the Society of Antiquaries of Scotland 72: 44-55

facts_added.fact: The 1980 East Tullos experiment near Aberdeen burned a timber-laced wall 9.4 m long, 4 m wide and 2.45 m high for about 28 hours and produced only about 3 kg of vitrified stone.
facts_added.source: Ralston 1986, Proceedings of the Society of Antiquaries of Scotland 116: 17-40

facts_added.fact: The natural reactors operated about 1,950 million years ago, when uranium-235 made up about 3.7% of uranium (235U/238U); the reactions lasted 85,000 to 620,000 years depending on the zone; natural reactors are known only in the Franceville basin of Gabon (Oklo, Okelobondo, Bangombe); water acted as the neutron moderator.
facts_added.source: Gauthier-Lafaye et al. 1996, Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta 60: 4831-4852, doi:10.1016/S0016-7037(96)00245-1

facts_added.fact: Xenon isotopes in the Oklo/Okelobondo ores show the reactors cycled: about 30 minutes active, then about 2.5 hours dormant, for about 150,000 years in the zone studied.
facts_added.source: Meshik et al. 2004, Physical Review Letters 93: 182302, doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.93.182302

facts_added.fact: Paul Kuroda, a chemist at the University of Arkansas, predicted in 1956 that a natural uranium deposit could sustain a chain reaction; the Oklo reactors were found in 1972, sixteen years later.
facts_added.source: Kuroda 1956, Journal of Chemical Physics 25: 781-782, doi:10.1063/1.1743058; Encyclopedia of Arkansas, Paul Kazuo Kuroda

facts_added.fact: Oklo's isotopes limit any change of the fine-structure constant over about two billion years to about one part in ten million (Damour and Dyson: between minus 0.9 and plus 1.2 parts in ten million).
facts_added.source: Shlyakhter 1976, Nature 264: 340, doi:10.1038/264340a0; Damour & Dyson 1996, Nuclear Physics B 480: 37-54, doi:10.1016/S0550-3213(96)00467-1

facts_added.fact: Plutonium from nuclear weapons tests appears in the varved sediments of Crawford Lake from about 1950 and peaks in the mid-1960s, proposed as the primary marker of the Anthropocene; annual plutonium fallout records also exist in ten Arctic and Antarctic ice cores.
facts_added.source: McCarthy et al. 2023, The Anthropocene Review 10: 146-176, doi:10.1177/20530196221149281; Arienzo et al. 2016, Environmental Science & Technology 50: 7066-7073, doi:10.1021/acs.est.6b01108

facts_added.fact: Plutonium-239 has a half-life of about 24,100 years, so about 89% of it would remain after 4,000 years.
facts_added.source: Evaluated nuclear data (ENSDF/NNDC), plutonium-239 half-life 24,110 years

shots.say: In a jewel made for the boy king Tutankhamun, a beetle of yellow-green glass glows in gold.
shots.draw: THE HERO IMAGE, whole and lit from the first frame: Tutankhamun's pectoral (Cairo JE 61884) drawn large, right of centre, on a dark museum ground under a soft spotlight. Gold frame; at its heart a translucent yellow-green scarab that glows from inside; falcon wings spread left and right in rows of blue, turquoise and red feathers; above the scarab a little boat carrying the eye of Horus between two rearing cobras, and over it a silver moon disc on a gold crescent; below, lotus and papyrus flowers and a fringe of drop pendants. Kept right of x 960 in the top 280 units so the hook title stays clear. After the title clears, labels: 'Tutankhamun's pectoral' and 'the scarab: desert glass', with a thin leader line to the scarab.

shots.say: The same glass lies scattered on the sand of the Sahara.
shots.draw: The Great Sand Sea at dawn: long dune ridges in layers (back ones dim), a corridor of bare pale rock in front; yellow-green lumps of glass lie on it and catch the light one after another (small glows); one person for scale. A small locator map in a rounded window, top right: Egypt with the Nile and a gold dot for the glass field. Label 'the Great Sand Sea, Egypt'.

shots.say: Something melted that desert. Some modern writers see in it the mark of an atomic blast, and read passages of old epics, such as the Mahabharata, as accounts of such weapons.
shots.draw: The same dunes at dusk, wider. Over the far ridges a mushroom cloud rises, drawn only as a dotted lilac outline (the 'claimed' style), with the label 'an atomic blast?'. No scripture is drawn or quoted: a small dotted lilac tag at the side reads 'a modern reading'.

shots.say: They point to more clues: black glass in Arabia, skeletons in an Indus city, melted walls, and a nuclear reactor in Africa.
shots.draw: A map from Scotland to the Indus and down to Gabon (about 12 W to 75 E, 5 S to 60 N). The glass field in Egypt already glows gold; then four pins pop in the order named, each with a tiny icon: Wabar in the Empty Quarter (a ring crater), Mohenjo-daro on the Indus (a city grid), Scotland (a wall), Oklo in Gabon (a small atom). Labels: 'Great Sand Sea', 'Wabar', 'Mohenjo-daro', 'Scotland', 'Oklo'.

shots.say: So was there a nuclear war before history? And how would we know?
shots.draw: Back on the dark ground: the glowing scarab small at the centre; five faint lights around it (the five clues); behind, the dotted lilac mushroom outline faint; a large lilac question mark rises above. The title card comes over this panel.

shots.draw: A cut across the dunes: two dune ridges 100 m high (dimension line '100 m') with a corridor of bare rock between them; a person (1.7 m) tiny on the corridor; yellow-green lumps glint on the rock. Closer, at the right, one big lump with a tag 'up to 4.5 kg'.

shots.say: It is almost pure silica, the stuff of sand and window glass.
shots.draw: Three things in a row on a dark shelf, built as named: a heap of sand, a pane of window glass, a lump of desert glass; one label 'silica' joins them; a small tag 'about 98% silica'.

shots.say: And a nuclear blast can melt sand into glass, too: in 1945, the first atomic test, Trinity, turned the sand of New Mexico into green glass.
shots.draw: New Mexico desert at dawn: the steel test tower (about 30 m) with a flash at its top; the ground around its foot turns into a crust of green glass that spreads in a ring; labels 'Trinity, New Mexico, 1945' and 'green glass: trinitite'.

lines: [d:build][act:curious, the method][tune:rise]So how old is the yellow ^glass? [p:0.93][act:explaining, clear]A few uranium atoms inside it split on their own, now and then, and each one leaves a tiny scar, a ^track. [act:explaining, a simple picture]Count the tracks, like tally marks, and you can read@present the ^age. [p:0.9][act:the big number, slow][tune:fall]About twenty-nine million ^years.

[d:reveal][act:the twist, delighted]So the glass ^is nuclear, in a ^way: [act:the payoff][tune:fall]it keeps time with its own ^uranium. [act:the point, plain][tune:fall]And it is more than twenty million years older than the first ^humans.

shots.say: So how old is the yellow glass? A few uranium atoms inside it split on their own, now and then, and each one leaves a tiny scar, a track. Count the tracks, like tally marks, and you can read the age. About twenty-nine million years.
shots.draw: A round magnifier over the glass: inside, a few uranium atoms as small gold dots; one by one an atom splits into two fragments that fly apart and leave a straight dark scratch (a track). At the right, tally marks gather in groups of five as each track appears; then the tag 'about 29 million years' pops.

shots.say: So the glass is nuclear, in a way: it keeps time with its own uranium. And it is more than twenty million years older than the first humans.
shots.draw: A time line from 30 million years ago to today: the glass at 29 million (gold marker with a small atom icon, 'the yellow glass'); near the right end, a tick at about 2.8 million 'the first humans' (the genus Homo); a bracket between them 'more than 20 million years'.

lines: [d:reveal][act:the crux, curious][tune:rise]Then what melted ^it? [p:0.93][act:explaining, clear]Tiny zircon crystals in the glass keep traces of a mineral that, in nature, forms only under the crushing shock of an ^impact. [act:explaining, vivid]The melt passed two thousand seven hundred and fifty ^degrees, more than twice as hot as ^lava, [act:the third clue][tune:fall]and the bedrock nearby holds quartz scarred by the same ^shock.

[d:build][act:fair, the open part]But no crater has been ^confirmed; [act:plain, a small shrug][tune:fall]one candidate, ^Kebira, failed the ^tests. [act:fair, the challenger's case]So some argue for an ^airburst, a rock exploding in the sky whose heat melted the sand ^below. [act:the reply, precise][tune:fall]The shocked bedrock points instead to a real impact, its crater worn ^away.

shots.say: Then what melted it? Tiny zircon crystals in the glass keep traces of a mineral that, in nature, forms only under the crushing shock of an impact. The melt passed two thousand seven hundred and fifty degrees, more than twice as hot as lava, and the bedrock nearby holds quartz scarred by the same shock.
shots.draw: Three clues drawn in turn, left to right: a zircon crystal under a lens, its inside grainy with tiny bright specks ('a shock mineral'); a thermometer whose bar rises past 'lava, about 1,200 °C' to 'the melt, over 2,750 °C'; a grain of quartz crossed by fine parallel lines ('shocked quartz').

shots.say: But no crater has been confirmed; one candidate, Kebira, failed the tests. So some argue for an airburst, a rock exploding in the sky whose heat melted the sand below. The shocked bedrock points instead to a real impact, its crater worn away.
shots.draw: Two ways to melt a desert, side by side over one ground line: left, a rock falling into a crater drawn dashed ('an impact, crater worn away?'); right, a fireball high in the sky with heat rays reaching down and the sand glowing beneath ('an airburst?'). Over both: 'no crater confirmed'. A small ring 'Kebira' with a red cross pops on 'failed the tests'.

lines: [d:calm][act:storytelling, warm]About three thousand three hundred years ago, an Egyptian jeweller carved a piece of it into the scarab of a jewel for the boy king ^Tutankhamun. [act:storytelling]Howard ^Carter, who found the tomb, took it for ^chalcedony, a common ^stone. [p:0.93][act:the reveal, delighted][tune:fall]In the {1990s|nineteen nineties}, the mineralogist Vincenzo de ^Michele saw what it ^was: desert@noun ^glass.
[d:tension][act:the landing, quiet wonder][tune:fall]A pharaoh wore a splash of a cosmic ^blast, [act:the kicker, dry][tune:fall]millions of years older than his ^kingdom.

shots.say: About three thousand three hundred years ago, an Egyptian jeweller carved a piece of it into the scarab of a jewel for the boy king Tutankhamun. Howard Carter, who found the tomb, took it for chalcedony, a common stone. In the 1990s, the mineralogist Vincenzo de Michele saw what it was: desert glass.
shots.draw: The pectoral again, closer on its scarab; beside it a museum card on a pin, 'chalcedony', which a red line strikes through; a gold tag replaces it: 'desert glass, 1990s'.

shots.say: A pharaoh wore a splash of a cosmic blast, millions of years older than his kingdom.
shots.draw: The scarab glows at the left; at the right a raw lump of the same glass on sand catches the same light; between them a thin gold line; tags 'about 3,300 years ago' and '29 million years old'.

lines: [d:calm][act:storytelling, placing it]In {1932|nineteen thirty-two}, the British explorer ^Philby crossed Arabia's Empty Quarter, the biggest sea of sand on ^Earth, looking for a lost ^city. [act:vivid][tune:fall]His guides spoke of ^Wabar, a city of ruins and ^iron, deep in the ^dunes.
[d:build][act:the arrival, wonder]He found no ^city. [act:vivid][tune:fall]He found ^craters, ringed with black ^glass, [act:a small smile][tune:fall]and took them for an old ^volcano.

shots.say: His guides spoke of Wabar, a city of ruins and iron, deep in the dunes.
shots.draw: A map of the Arabian Peninsula (about 35 to 60 E, 12 to 31 N): the Empty Quarter shaded as sand; Riyadh; a gold pin 'Wabar'; Philby's crossing drawn as a dotted line (schematic) with the tag 'Philby, 1932'; above Wabar a dotted lilac tag 'a lost city?'. Scale bar 300 km.
shots.reuse: wabar shot 1, its map of Arabia

shots.say: He found no city. He found craters, ringed with black glass, and took them for an old volcano.
shots.draw: Dunes at dusk; three camels with riders arrive along a crest; over the far dunes a ruined city skyline drawn only as a dotted lilac outline fades under a veil on 'no city'; in front, two shallow craters with dark rims of black glass beads appear on 'craters'; a dotted lilac tag 'a volcano?'.

lines: [d:build][act:the correction, precise]In fact, they were punched into the sand by a falling iron ^meteorite. [act:the size, wonder]The biggest crater is a hundred and sixteen metres ^across, [act:the detail][tune:fall]and the largest piece of iron, the Camel's ^Hump, weighs about two ^tonnes. [p:0.93][act:the number that matters, slow][tune:fall]The blast released about as much energy as the Hiroshima ^bomb.

[d:reveal][act:fair, the test][tune:rise]So what does@verb the ground ^hold? [act:listing, clear][tune:level]Black glass made of dune sand and meteorite ^iron, [tune:level]droplets of iron and nickel ^metal, [tune:fall]and sand grains shocked into ^rock. [p:0.93][act:the point, plain][tune:fall]Nothing a falling meteorite can't ^explain.

shots.say: In fact, they were punched into the sand by a falling iron meteorite. The biggest crater is a hundred and sixteen metres across, and the largest piece of iron, the Camel's Hump, weighs about two tonnes.
shots.draw: A cut through the sand: an iron meteorite streaks in from the upper left and the crater opens, 116 m across (dimension line); below it, a football pitch drawn to the same scale (about 105 m) for comparison. At the right, the Camel's Hump, a rounded lump of iron, beside a car: 'about 2 tonnes'.

shots.say: The blast released about as much energy as the Hiroshima bomb.
shots.draw: Two equal flashes side by side on a dark ground: 'Wabar, a falling iron' and 'Hiroshima, 1945'; an equals sign between them; label 'about the same energy'.

shots.say: So what does the ground hold? Black glass made of dune sand and meteorite iron, droplets of iron and nickel metal, and sand grains shocked into rock. Nothing a falling meteorite can't explain.
shots.draw: Under a lens, three finds pop as named: a bead of black glass with sand grains in it; inside it, tiny bright droplets of iron and nickel; a block of white 'instant rock' (sand shocked into stone). A green tick by each; then a bracket 'a falling iron explains it'.

lines: [d:build][act:the method, curious]Then came the ^date. [p:0.9][act:explaining, the analogy]Grains of sand work like tiny ^batteries: lying in the dark, they slowly charge up from natural ^radiation. [act:the key step]The heat of the impact emptied them all at ^once. [p:0.93][act:the result, clear][tune:fall]From the charge they hold today, the fire was about three hundred years ^ago.
[d:aside][act:wry, light]And the dunes keep ^moving: [act:plain][tune:fall]by {2008|two thousand eight}, one of the craters had vanished under the ^sand.

shots.say: Then came the date. Grains of sand work like tiny batteries: lying in the dark, they slowly charge up from natural radiation. The heat of the impact emptied them all at once. From the charge they hold today, the fire was about three hundred years ago.
shots.draw: A grain of sand beside a battery gauge: the gauge fills segment by segment ('charging in the dark'); a flash ('the impact') empties it at once; it refills slowly; a time line 1600 to today with a gold band about 1670 to 1750: 'about 300 years ago'.
shots.reuse: wabar_m(), the grain of sand as a battery

shots.say: And the dunes keep moving: by 2008, one of the craters had vanished under the sand.
shots.draw: Two craters seen from the side in the sand sheet; a big dune creeps in from the left (arrow 'dunes move 1 to 2 m a year') and covers the smaller crater; tag '2008: buried'.

lines: [d:tension][act:the landing, warm][tune:fall]A blast as big as Hiroshima's, with no bomb at ^all. [act:the last word, a small smile][tune:fall]Philby went looking for a lost city, and found a fallen ^star.

shots.say: A blast as big as Hiroshima's, with no bomb at all. Philby went looking for a lost city, and found a fallen star.
shots.draw: Night over the Empty Quarter: stars, a shooting star streaks down towards the dunes; a small camp fire with two figures and a camel; the crater rim catches the starlight.

lines: [d:calm][act:storytelling, placing it]Mohenjo-daro, on the Indus River in today's ^Pakistan, was one of the great cities of the world about four and a half thousand years ^ago. [act:vivid, a picture][tune:fall]Straight streets, houses@noun of fired ^brick, wells and covered ^drains, for tens of thousands of ^people.

[d:build][act:the claim at its strongest, fair]Online, you'll read@present that skeletons lay in its ^streets, some holding ^hands, as if death came in an ^instant. [act:the claim, fair][tune:fall]And that their bones were ^radioactive.

shots.say: Straight streets, houses of fired brick, wells and covered drains, for tens of thousands of people.
shots.draw: The city from above at an angle: a grid of straight streets between blocks of brick houses with courtyards; round wells pop; a covered drain runs along a street; the citadel mound behind; small people in the streets. Labels: 'fired brick', 'wells', 'covered drains'. A locator map in a rounded window, top left: the Indus to the Arabian Sea, a gold pin 'Mohenjo-daro, Pakistan'.

shots.say: Online, you'll read that skeletons lay in its streets, some holding hands, as if death came in an instant. And that their bones were radioactive.
shots.draw: The same street at night, drawn only in dotted lilac lines (the claim); a stack of paperback books at the side, dotted; a dotted tag 'the story told online'; a dotted radiation trefoil with a question mark: 'radioactive?'. No bodies are drawn.

lines: [d:build][act:the method, curious][tune:rise]So what did the excavators actually write ^down? [p:0.93][act:explaining, plain]Between {1922|nineteen twenty-two} and {1931|nineteen thirty-one}, they found about thirty-seven skeletons in houses@noun and ^lanes, in a few small ^groups. [act:gently, with care]Fourteen lay together in one ^room. [act:quieter, with care][tune:fall]Nine lay in another quarter, at least five of them ^children.

[d:reveal][act:the twist, careful]But they were not all found at the same ^level. [p:0.93][act:explaining, a picture]Digging down through a city is like turning back the pages of a ^book: [act:the payoff][tune:fall]these groups lie on different pages, some in the rubble of houses@noun already in ^ruins.

shots.say: So what did the excavators actually write down? Between 1922 and 1931, they found about thirty-seven skeletons in houses and lanes, in a few small groups. Fourteen lay together in one room. Nine lay in another quarter, at least five of them children.
shots.draw: An excavation plan of the city in pale lines, schematic, its quarters lettered (HR, DK, VS) as tidy grids of rooms and lanes; the groups appear as small numbered discs, never as bodies, where Dales (1964) places them: in HR, '14' in a room of House V, '3' in a courtyard and '1' in Deadman Lane; in DK, '9' in Block 10A (a soft note: 'at least 5 children') and '2' on the stairs of a well room; in VS, '6' in a lane. The small groups pop on 'small groups', the 14 and the 9 as they are named. A field notebook beside it: '1922 to 1931' and 'about 37'.

shots.say: But they were not all found at the same level. Digging down through a city is like turning back the pages of a book: these groups lie on different pages, some in the rubble of houses already in ruins.
shots.draw: A cut through the mound, schematic: debris on top, the later city with its broken brick walls standing up into the debris, the earlier city below (labels 'debris', 'later', 'earlier'). The numbered discs sit at different depths, as Dales (1964) reads the records: the 6 in a lane between walls, the 14 partly over the top of a ruined wall, the 3 and the 1 in the debris of places already in ruins (on 'rubble'); the 9 lower down, drawn dashed (Mackay doubted its date). At the left an open book whose pages turn back one by one; tag 'different levels, different times'.

lines: [d:reveal][act:storytelling, even]In the {1940s|nineteen forties}, the archaeologist Mortimer ^Wheeler read@past them as victims of a ^massacre. [act:the turn, plain]Yet even the first excavators had ^disagreed: [tune:level]one saw a ^tragedy, [tune:fall]another, people buried ^quickly. [p:0.93][act:the conclusion, plain]In {1964|nineteen sixty-four}, the archaeologist George ^Dales went back through the records@noun. [act:fair, careful]A couple may have been killed where they ^lay. [act:the payoff, plain][tune:fall]But he found no layer of destruction, and no sign of a great ^fire.

[d:build][act:the second claim, firm][tune:rise]And the ^radioactivity? [p:0.93][act:plain, careful][tune:fall]No published study of these bones reports a radiation ^measurement: [act:counting off][tune:level]no ^laboratory, [tune:level]no ^sample, [tune:fall]no ^number@count.

shots.say: In the 1940s, the archaeologist Mortimer Wheeler read them as victims of a massacre. Yet even the first excavators had disagreed: one saw a tragedy, another, people buried quickly. In 1964, the archaeologist George Dales went back through the records. A couple may have been killed where they lay. But he found no layer of destruction, and no sign of a great fire.
shots.draw: Documents on a desk under a lamp: a 1940s report with a dotted tag 'a massacre?'; two field notebooks open side by side, 'a tragedy' and 'buried quickly'; then Dales's 1964 paper slides in front; on 'a couple', a small dashed note 'a couple killed in place?'; then two stamps pop as said: 'no destruction layer', 'no great fire'. No bodies are drawn.

shots.say: And the radioactivity? No published study of these bones reports a radiation measurement: no laboratory, no sample, no number.
shots.draw: Three dashed boxes, empty, labelled as said: 'laboratory', 'sample', 'number', each with a faint lilac question mark; above them a radiation counter whose needle rests at zero; label 'no measurement published'.

lines: [d:calm][act:the bigger picture, gentle]The city did not end in a ^flash. [p:0.93][act:explaining][tune:fall]From about three thousand nine hundred years ago, as the monsoon ^weakened, the great Indus cities emptied slowly, over ^generations. [act:the landing, tender][tune:fall]These were people, children among them, and they deserve their real ^story.

shots.say: The city did not end in a flash. From about three thousand nine hundred years ago, as the monsoon weakened, the great Indus cities emptied slowly, over generations. These were people, children among them, and they deserve their real story.
shots.draw: The Indus plain at dusk: monsoon clouds thin out across the sky, the river narrows; settlement lights fade on the plain and new ones appear further east along a time line 'about 3,900 years ago' ('emptied over generations'); in front, a family walks away along the river bank, a child holding a parent's hand.

lines: [d:calm][act:storytelling, placing it]On hilltops across Scotland stand the ruins of Iron Age forts whose stone walls have melted into ^glass. [act:explaining, plain]Archaeologists call them vitrified ^forts, [act:the number][tune:fall]and Europe has some two hundred of ^them.
[d:build][act:the claim, fair]To melt rock, you need about a thousand degrees, for ^hours. [act:the challenger's case, fair][tune:fall]To some writers, only an atomic flash could do ^that.

shots.say: Archaeologists call them vitrified forts, and Europe has some two hundred of them.
shots.draw: A Scottish hill at dusk in layers of dim ridges; on its top the low ring of a ruined rampart, patches of it glinting like dark glass; a walker for scale; tag 'about 200 vitrified forts in Europe'.

shots.say: To melt rock, you need about a thousand degrees, for hours. To some writers, only an atomic flash could do that.
shots.draw: Close on a chunk of the rampart: stones fused together by dark glass with bubbles and drips; a thermometer climbs to 'about 1,000 °C' and a clock face 'for hours'; then a dotted lilac flash outline with 'an atomic flash?'.

lines: [d:build][act:storytelling, delighted]In March {1937|nineteen thirty-seven}, the archaeologist Gordon ^Childe and the mining engineer Wallace ^Thorneycroft put it to the ^test. [p:0.93][act:explaining, step by step]At Thorneycroft's colliery near Stirling, they built a short wall like the ancient ^ones: stone rubble, laced with ^timber. [act:the action, vivid][tune:fall]Then they set it on ^fire.

[d:reveal][act:the result, wonder]Twenty hours later, it was still ^smouldering. [p:0.93][act:the reveal, slow]When it cooled, the stones inside had fused into ^glass, [act:the detail, delighted][tune:fall]holding the casts of burnt timber and bits of ^charcoal.

shots.say: In March 1937, the archaeologist Gordon Childe and the mining engineer Wallace Thorneycroft put it to the test. At Thorneycroft's colliery near Stirling, they built a short wall like the ancient ones: stone rubble, laced with timber. Then they set it on fire.
shots.draw: A colliery yard (a pit headframe in the dim background); the experimental wall drawn as a cut-away block 3.7 m long and 1.8 m high (12 by 6 feet): brick faces, rubble core, timber beams laced through it, built course by course; two figures in 1930s coats beside it for scale; labels 'Plean colliery, 1937' and 'rubble laced with timber'; on 'set it on fire', flames climb the wall.

shots.say: Twenty hours later, it was still smouldering. When it cooled, the stones inside had fused into glass, holding the casts of burnt timber and bits of charcoal.
shots.draw: The same wall after the fire, cut open: a clock runs round, '20 hours later'; the core has fused into dark glass (amber-black, glossy) with hollow casts where the beams were and black specks of charcoal; labels 'fused into glass', 'casts of timber', 'charcoal'.

lines: [d:reveal][act:fair, the caveat]It isn't ^easy. [p:0.93][act:explaining]A bigger wall, burned near Aberdeen in {1980|nineteen eighty}, gave only about three kilograms of ^glass. [act:the point][tune:fall]It takes the right stone, the right draught and a long, fierce ^fire.

shots.say: It isn't easy. A bigger wall, burned near Aberdeen in 1980, gave only about three kilograms of glass. It takes the right stone, the right draught and a long, fierce fire.
shots.draw: A longer timber-laced wall (9.4 m long, 2.45 m high) with a big fire; then, small beside it, a hand-sized heap of glassy lumps on a scale 'about 3 kg'; tag '1980, near Aberdeen'; three small icons pop as named: a stone, a gust of air, a flame.

lines: [d:calm][act:the open question, honest]Why the forts burned is still ^argued: [tune:level]an ^attack, [tune:level]a ^ritual, [tune:fall]or builders hardening their own ^walls. [act:the landing, plain][tune:fall]But the heat was real, and the fuel was ^wood.

shots.say: Why the forts burned is still argued: an attack, a ritual, or builders hardening their own walls. But the heat was real, and the fuel was wood.
shots.draw: Three dashed tags with small pictures pop as named: 'an attack?' (torches at a gate), 'a ritual?' (a ring of fire), 'builders?' (a mason's trowel); below them, logs glow in a fire and the label 'the fuel: wood'.

lines: [d:intrigue][act:storytelling, a hint of wonder]In {1972|nineteen seventy-two}, French engineers checking uranium ore from ^Oklo, in Gabon, found that some of it had already been burned in a nuclear ^reactor. [act:the reveal, slow][tune:fall]A reactor that had shut down about two billion years ^earlier.

[d:calm][p:0.93][act:patient, laying out the clue]Uranium comes in two main kinds, and only the rare one splits ^easily. [p:0.9][act:the key number, slow]Anywhere on Earth, about seven uranium atoms in a thousand are that ^kind. [act:dropping the clue, pointed]Oklo's had ^less. [act:quieter][tune:fall]Some samples, much ^less.

shots.say: A reactor that had shut down about two billion years earlier.
shots.draw: Left: a map from France down to Gabon (about 10 W to 25 E, 5 S to 50 N) with a gold pin 'Oklo, Gabon' and a pin 'Pierrelatte, France' joined by a dotted line 'uranium ore, 1972'. Right: a time line from 2.5 billion years ago to today builds; a gold glow at about 2 billion: 'the reactor'; tiny marks 'first animals' near 0.6 billion and 'today'.

shots.say: Uranium comes in two main kinds, and only the rare one splits easily. Anywhere on Earth, about seven uranium atoms in a thousand are that kind. Oklo's had less. Some samples, much less.
shots.draw: Two grids of 1,000 small dots (40 by 25): left 'anywhere on Earth', 7 dots light gold; right 'Oklo', only 4 light; tag 'about 7 in 1,000'.

lines: [d:build][act:the claim, fair, a touch playful]Online, the answer is ^easy: an ancient nuclear ^plant, built by ^someone. [p:0.93][act:the reply, plain][tune:fall]But two billion years ago, there were no animals on Earth at all, let alone ^engineers.

[d:build][act:the turn, explaining with relish]The real answer is an ^hourglass. [p:0.93][act:explaining, an everyday picture]The rare kind of uranium decays faster than the common one, so its share keeps ^shrinking, like sand running out of the top of the ^glass. [p:0.9][act:the key number, slow]Two billion years ago, it was about five times ^higher, [act:the payoff, delighted][tune:fall]close@adj to the fuel of a modern ^reactor.

shots.say: Online, the answer is easy: an ancient nuclear plant, built by someone. But two billion years ago, there were no animals on Earth at all, let alone engineers.
shots.draw: A dotted lilac outline of a power plant with cooling towers in a jungle ('an ancient plant?'); then, beside it, the real scene: a bare coast two billion years ago under a hazy sky, low domes of microbial mats in the shallows, not one animal; tag 'no animals yet'.

shots.say: The real answer is an hourglass. The rare kind of uranium decays faster than the common one, so its share keeps shrinking, like sand running out of the top of the glass. Two billion years ago, it was about five times higher, close to the fuel of a modern reactor.
shots.draw: An hourglass with gold sand running down, at the left; at the right a chart: the share of the rare uranium falls from about 3.6% two billion years ago to 0.72% today (curve draws itself); a pale band 'modern reactor fuel, 3 to 5%' across the chart; the two-billion point sits inside it.

lines: [d:reveal][act:building, step by step]Then groundwater seeped into the uranium ^seams. [p:0.93][act:explaining, a simple picture]Water slows the neutrons that split atoms, and slow neutrons split them far ^better, the way a gentle throw is easier to ^catch. [act:the payoff, a small wonder][tune:fall]The rock went critical, by ^itself.

[d:build][act:delighted, lean in]And it ^pulsed. [p:0.93][act:laying out the rhythm][tune:level]The heat boiled the water away, and the reaction ^stopped; [act:the other half][tune:fall]the water seeped back, and it started ^again. [p:0.9][act:precise][tune:level]About thirty minutes@time ^on, [tune:fall]two and a half hours ^off, for many thousands of ^years.

shots.say: Then groundwater seeped into the uranium seams. Water slows the neutrons that split atoms, and slow neutrons split them far better, the way a gentle throw is easier to catch. The rock went critical, by itself.
shots.draw: A cut through the ground: a dark seam of uranium ore between sandstone layers; blue groundwater seeps down into it; inside a lens, a fast neutron (red streak) slows in the water (blue zigzag), hits an atom that splits and throws out two more; the seam begins to glow: 'critical'.

shots.say: And it pulsed. The heat boiled the water away, and the reaction stopped; the water seeped back, and it started again. About thirty minutes on, two and a half hours off, for many thousands of years.
shots.draw: A chart that draws itself along a time axis in hours: glowing blocks 30 minutes long ('on') separated by gaps 2.5 hours long ('off'); a blue water level line falls during each block and refills in each gap; small puffs of steam.

lines: [d:aside][p:0.93][act:storytelling, admiring]In {1956|nineteen fifty-six}, the chemist Paul ^Kuroda had predicted that nature could run such a ^reactor. [act:the payoff, warm][tune:fall]Sixteen years before anyone found ^one.

[d:reveal][act:the twist, leaning in]And physicists still read@present it like a ^diary. [p:0.93][act:explaining][tune:level]Its atoms show that a constant of nature has changed by no more than about one part in ten million in two billion ^years, [tune:fall]and how a reactor's waste moves through ^rock. [act:the landing, slow][tune:fall]A nuclear reaction signs its work, and the signature ^lasts.

shots.say: In 1956, the chemist Paul Kuroda had predicted that nature could run such a reactor. Sixteen years before anyone found one.
shots.draw: A short time line 1950 to 1975: a paper pops at 1956 ('Kuroda's prediction'), the Oklo find at 1972; a bracket between them '16 years'.

shots.say: And physicists still read it like a diary. Its atoms show that a constant of nature has changed by no more than about one part in ten million in two billion years, and how a reactor's waste moves through rock. A nuclear reaction signs its work, and the signature lasts.
shots.draw: An open notebook glowing over the ore seam; from it two tags rise as named: 'a constant of nature: steady to about 1 in 10 million' (a level line), 'waste: stayed close by' (dots that barely spread from the seam); then a gold signature stroke draws itself across the seam.

lines: [d:verdict][act:stepping back, calm]So, let's weigh the ^clues. [act:the first, firm][tune:rise]The yellow glass, melted by a cosmic impact twenty-nine million years ^ago? [act:the verdict, measured][tune:fall]*Strong ^evidence*; [act:fair][tune:fall]only the crater is ^missing. [act:the second, steady][tune:rise]Wabar, an iron meteorite a few centuries ^ago? [act:the verdict, firm][tune:fall]*^Established*.

[d:verdict][act:the third, careful][tune:rise]The skeletons of Mohenjo-daro, killed in one ^blast? [act:the verdict, even][tune:fall]*Ruled ^out*. [act:the next][tune:rise]Radioactive ^bones? [act:the verdict, even][tune:fall]*Awaiting ^evidence*: [act:plain][tune:fall]nobody has published a ^measurement. [act:the fourth][tune:rise]Melted walls, from burning ^timber? [act:the verdict][tune:fall]*^Established*, [act:fair][tune:fall]though why they burned is an *open ^question*. [act:the last][tune:rise]Oklo, a natural ^reactor? [act:the verdict, confident][tune:fall]*^Established*.

shots.say: The yellow glass, melted by a cosmic impact twenty-nine million years ago? Strong evidence; only the crater is missing. Wabar, an iron meteorite a few centuries ago? Established.
shots.draw: A ledger board of five rows, each with a small picture at the left (a lump of yellow glass, a ring crater, a city grid, a wall, an atom); the first two rows light as named and their grade chips pop: 'Strong evidence', 'Established'.

shots.say: The skeletons of Mohenjo-daro, killed in one blast? Ruled out. Radioactive bones? Awaiting evidence: nobody has published a measurement. Melted walls, from burning timber? Established, though why they burned is an open question. Oklo, a natural reactor? Established.
shots.draw: Same ledger, the camera lower: row three gets two chips, 'Ruled out' (one blast) and 'Awaiting evidence' (radioactive bones); row four 'Established' with a small 'Open question' chip for why; row five 'Established'.

lines: [d:calm][p:0.95][act:the whole picture, weighing it][tune:rise]And an ancient nuclear ^war? [act:the verdict, level-headed][tune:fall]*Ruled ^out*. [act:explaining why, even][tune:fall]Each clue has a cause we can see at ^work, and the fingerprint a war would leave has never been ^found. [act:respectful, warm][tune:fall]We have weighed only glass, stone, bone and ^atoms; the epics belong to those who hold them ^sacred.

shots.say: And an ancient nuclear war? Ruled out. Each clue has a cause we can see at work, and the fingerprint a war would leave has never been found. We have weighed only glass, stone, bone and atoms; the epics belong to those who hold them sacred.
shots.draw: The five pictures of the ledger in a row, each now joined by its real cause (a falling rock, an iron meteorite, time and a weakening monsoon, a wood fire, groundwater); above them the dotted lilac mushroom outline and the chip 'Ruled out'; an empty dashed box 'the fingerprint'.

lines: [d:tension][act:what a bomb leaves, clear][tune:rise]What ^fingerprint? [p:0.93][act:explaining]The bomb tests of the {1950s|nineteen fifties} left plutonium in lake mud and polar ^ice, a thin layer that geologists use@verb to mark those ^years. [p:0.9][act:the key number]Plutonium loses half of itself only every twenty-four thousand ^years. [act:the payoff][tune:fall]A war four thousand years ago would still ^show.

[d:tension][act:what would settle it, inviting][tune:rise]What would change our ^minds? [act:clear, the test][tune:fall]Plutonium in a layer of lake mud or ice a few thousand years ^old, [act:the decisive part][tune:fall]found by two independent ^laboratories. [act:warm, a genuine open invitation][tune:fall]Find that, and we'll weigh it ^too.

shots.say: What fingerprint? The bomb tests of the 1950s left plutonium in lake mud and polar ice, a thin layer that geologists use to mark those years. Plutonium loses half of itself only every twenty-four thousand years. A war four thousand years ago would still show.
shots.draw: Left: a lake-mud core in fine yearly layers with a thin red band near the top, '1950s: plutonium'; beside it an ice core with the same band. Right: a decay curve for plutonium that halves every 24,000 years; a marker at 4,000 years shows almost nine tenths still there: 'still there'.

shots.say: What would change our minds? Plutonium in a layer of lake mud or ice a few thousand years old, found by two independent laboratories. Find that, and we'll weigh it too.
shots.draw: Three dashed boxes (tests not yet passed) fill as named: an atom with its fragments, 'plutonium'; a layer of lake mud and ice with a thin red band and the tag 'a few thousand years old', 'in lake mud or ice'; two lab flasks, 'two independent labs'.

lines: [d:calm][act:quiet, the image][tune:fall]In Egypt, a beetle of desert@noun glass still ^glows, [act:quiet wonder][tune:fall]a splash of a cosmic fire, millions of years older than any ^war. [act:the sign-off, warm][tune:fall]Weigh it ^yourself.

shots.say: In Egypt, a beetle of desert glass still glows, a splash of a cosmic fire, millions of years older than any war. Weigh it yourself.
shots.draw: Night: the pectoral on a plinth, the scarab glowing softly; behind it, faint dunes under the stars; the camera holds as the end card arrives.
